Getting started

Source: vignettes/mediamix.Rmd
mediamix.Rmd

mediamix turns raw marketing data into model-ready features. It does two things, and deliberately not a third: it converts media spend into carryover- and saturation-adjusted regressors, and it converts raw event logs into attributed customer journeys. It does not fit models. lm(), glmnet and brms already do that better than a marketing package would.

This vignette walks the whole arc on the media side: raw weekly spend, through diagnostics and transforms, to a fitted model, contributions and return on investment. It uses mm_weekly, three years of synthetic weekly spend, price and revenue for three geographies, generated from known parameters so that the estimates can be checked against the truth. Most of the work is on the north geography:

library(mediamix)
data(mm_weekly)

north <- mm_weekly[mm_weekly$geo == "north", ]
channels <- c("tv", "video", "search", "social", "display")
str(north[, c("date", channels, "price", "revenue")])
#> 'data.frame':    156 obs. of  8 variables:
#>  $ date   : Date, format: "2023-01-02" "2023-01-09" ...
#>  $ tv     : num  0 0 2193 0 0 ...
#>  $ video  : num  399 0 0 0 0 584 482 824 0 251 ...
#>  $ search : num  277 488 568 576 401 424 614 481 357 423 ...
#>  $ social : num  296 328 0 303 500 182 126 348 435 428 ...
#>  $ display: num  0 280 0 251 0 306 0 348 222 0 ...
#>  $ price  : num  22.1 25 25.3 25 26.8 ...
#>  $ revenue: num  27130 20433 20481 20565 17574 ...

Look before you transform

Many marketing mix projects fail for reasons visible in the data before any model is fitted. diagnose_media() checks for five of them: channels that move together, channels that barely vary, channels that are dark (spend nothing) in most weeks, an erratic cost per mille when impressions are supplied, and, given a date column, rows out of time order, repeated weeks and gaps, none of which adstock notices, since it takes adjacent rows as adjacent weeks. With by = "geo" it runs each check within each geography and reports the worst case.

diagnose_media(mm_weekly, media = channels, by = "geo", date = "date")
#> 
#> ── Media diagnostics
#> 468 observations across 3 series, 5 channels
#> Time index: every series is in order, with one row per period and no gaps.
#> ✔ No structural problems found.
#> 
#> Inspect $variation, $collinearity, $correlations, $dates.

Nothing structural is wrong here, which is what you would expect from synthetic data. On real data this is where you learn that two channels were planned together and their coefficients will therefore flip sign on small changes to the specification. The detail is in the elements the printout names, starting with the spend statistics in $variation:

d <- diagnose_media(mm_weekly, media = channels, by = "geo")
d$variation
#>   channel   mean    sd     cv distinct zero_share low_variation
#> 1      tv 1700.5 881.7 0.5096      131     0.1474         FALSE
#> 2   video  336.3 308.6 0.8939       84     0.4167         FALSE
#> 3  search  487.1 115.6 0.2286      118     0.0000         FALSE
#> 4  social  251.2 174.9 0.6613      101     0.2756         FALSE
#> 5 display  188.1 149.3 0.7584       88     0.3333         FALSE
#>   heavily_flighted usable
#> 1            FALSE   TRUE
#> 2            FALSE   TRUE
#> 3            FALSE   TRUE
#> 4            FALSE   TRUE
#> 5            FALSE   TRUE

With by supplied, cv, distinct and zero_share report the worst case across series, which is what you want from a diagnostic, while mean and sd are averages over the series. So read zero_share, the share of weeks with no spend, as the worst geography’s rate, not an overall average. video goes dark in 42% of weeks in its worst geography and display in 33%. That is normal, because media is flighted (bought in bursts with gaps between them), but it means those channels carry less information than 156 weeks per geography suggests.

Carryover

Advertising does not stop working the week it runs. Adstock spreads each period’s spend forward with geometric decay, using a set of weights called the kernel.

spend <- c(100, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0)
round(adstock_geometric(spend, decay = 0.5), 2)
#> [1] 50.00 25.00 12.50  6.25  3.12  1.56

By default the kernel’s weights sum to one, so the burst of 100 is spread out rather than repeated: half of it lands in the week of spend, a quarter in the week after, and so on. The section on normalisation below says why that matters.

Practitioners think in half-lives, not decay coefficients, so the package provides the translation:

theta <- decay_from_half_life(3)   # a three-week half-life on weekly data
theta
#> [1] 0.7937
half_life(theta)
#> [1] 3
effective_window(theta, coverage = 0.90)
#> [1] 10

decay_from_half_life(3) is the weekly decay for a three-week half-life, and half_life() converts it back. The last line says that carryover with this half-life needs 10 weeks to deliver 90% of its effect, which is how you decide whether truncating the kernel (the max_lag argument) costs you anything, and whether 156 weeks of data can identify a carryover this long at all.

Normalisation changes what your coefficient means

normalise is the argument that most often changes an answer without anyone noticing, so it is explicit rather than implied.

constant <- rep(100, 50)
tail(adstock_geometric(constant, decay = 0.8), 1)
#> [1] 100
tail(adstock_geometric(constant, decay = 0.8, normalise = FALSE), 1)
#> [1] 500

Normalised, the kernel sums to 1: once the filter has filled up, a constant spend of 100 adstocks to 100, the series level is preserved, and the fitted coefficient reads as the effect of one unit of media. Unnormalised (raw Koyck accumulation), the same series accumulates to 100 / (1 - 0.8), and the coefficient reads as the effect of one unit of accumulated media. Both are defensible. Comparing a coefficient fitted one way against a coefficient fitted the other is not.

mediamix defaults to normalised, as does the Bayesian media mix model of Jin et al. (2017). Robyn’s geometric adstock does not, so if you are reconciling against Robyn, set normalise = FALSE.

Dark weeks

Media data is full of zero-spend weeks, and carryover has to survive them:

flighted <- c(100, 100, 0, 0, 0, 0, 100)
round(adstock_geometric(flighted, decay = 0.6), 2)
#> [1] 40.00 64.00 38.40 23.04 13.82  8.29 44.98

Carryover decays across the gap rather than resetting, and the new burst adds to what is left.

Delayed peaks

A geometric kernel always peaks in the period of spend. Television and out-of-home often do not, and no decay rate fixes that. Weibull adstock with type = "pdf" can, and so can the delayed kernel of Jin et al. (2017), whose peak is read directly in weeks. The three kernels’ weights over eight weeks:

w_geo <- adstock_weights(8, decay = 0.6)
w_wei <- adstock_weights_weibull(8, shape = 2, scale = 3, type = "pdf")
w_del <- adstock_weights_delayed(8, decay = 0.6, peak = 2)
round(rbind(geometric = w_geo, weibull = w_wei, delayed = w_del), 3)
#>            [,1]  [,2]  [,3]  [,4]  [,5]  [,6]  [,7]  [,8]
#> geometric 0.407 0.244 0.146 0.088 0.053 0.032 0.019 0.011
#> weibull   0.203 0.290 0.250 0.153 0.070 0.025 0.007 0.001
#> delayed   0.052 0.243 0.405 0.243 0.052 0.004 0.000 0.000
which.max(w_wei)
#> [1] 2

The first column is the week of spend. The Weibull kernel’s largest weight is in column 2, 1 week after the spend, and the delayed kernel’s is 2 weeks after it. The three shapes side by side:

cols <- mm_palette(3)
ink <- mm_palette(role = "ink")
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 1), bg = ink[["surface"]], fg = ink[["axis"]])
matplot(0:7, cbind(w_geo, w_wei, w_del), type = "o", pch = 19, lty = 1,
        lwd = 2, col = cols, xlab = "Weeks after spend",
        ylab = "Share of the effect", las = 1, bty = "n",
        col.axis = ink[["muted"]], col.lab = ink[["secondary"]])
legend("topright", c("geometric, decay 0.6", "Weibull pdf, shape 2",
                     "delayed, peak at week 2"),
       col = cols, lwd = 2, pch = 19, bty = "n", text.col = ink[["secondary"]])

par(op)

Saturation

Adstock says when money works. Saturation says how hard it works at the margin. saturate_hill() maps media onto a share of the channel’s ceiling, between 0 and 1. Its half_max is the spend at which the response reaches half its ceiling, which is interpretable in the units you actually budget in. Its shape sets the form of the curve: shape = 1, the default, is concave, and shape > 1 produces the threshold effect below which media barely registers. Both forms at six levels of spend, with half_max at 100,000:

levels <- c(0, 25, 50, 100, 200, 400) * 1000
round(rbind(
  concave = saturate_hill(levels, half_max = 100000),
  s_shape = saturate_hill(levels, half_max = 100000, shape = 3)
), 3)
#>         [,1]  [,2]  [,3] [,4]  [,5]  [,6]
#> concave    0 0.200 0.333  0.5 0.667 0.800
#> s_shape    0 0.015 0.111  0.5 0.889 0.985
grid_spend <- seq(0, 400000, by = 2000)
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 1), bg = ink[["surface"]], fg = ink[["axis"]])
plot(grid_spend / 1000, saturate_hill(grid_spend, half_max = 100000),
     type = "l", lwd = 2, col = cols[1], ylim = c(0, 1), las = 1, bty = "n",
     xlab = "Spend (thousands)", ylab = "Share of the ceiling",
     col.axis = ink[["muted"]], col.lab = ink[["secondary"]])
lines(grid_spend / 1000, saturate_hill(grid_spend, 100000, shape = 3),
      lwd = 2, col = cols[2])
abline(v = 100, col = ink[["muted"]])
text(100, 0.05, "half_max", pos = 4, cex = 0.8, col = ink[["muted"]])
legend("bottomright", c("shape = 1, concave", "shape = 3, S-shaped"),
       col = cols[1:2], lwd = 2, bty = "n", text.col = ink[["secondary"]])

par(op)

Both curves reach half the ceiling at half_max. Below it the S-shaped curve barely registers; above it, the S-shaped curve closes on the ceiling faster than the concave one.

Composing carryover and saturation in the right order

Saturation goes after adstock. Saturating first puts each period’s spend through the curve in isolation, so carryover from earlier periods never counts towards saturation; with normalise = FALSE the kernel weights sum to more than one and carryover also lifts the result past the ceiling. media_transform() composes them in the right order and warns if asked to reverse it.

mm_weekly was generated from known parameters, attached as its "truth" attribute, so here we can transform each channel with the right decay, half_max and shape. A saturation list without a type uses the Hill curve. On real data you do not know these parameters: vignette("carryover") shows how to choose the decays, and vignette("tidymodels") how to tune them together with the saturation parameters.

spec holds one entry per channel, in the form media_transform() takes, and transform_plan() runs each channel’s column of the plan through its own entry:

truth <- attr(mm_weekly, "truth")

spec <- lapply(stats::setNames(channels, channels), function(ch) list(
  adstock = list(decay = truth$decay[[ch]]),
  saturation = list(half_max = truth$half_max[[ch]],
                    shape = truth$shape[[ch]])
))
transformed <- transform_plan(north, spec)[channels]
round(head(transformed, 4), 4)
#>       tv  video search social display
#> 1 0.0000 0.1663 0.3435 0.3175  0.0000
#> 2 0.0000 0.1225 0.5001 0.4202  0.2958
#> 3 0.0441 0.0890 0.5501 0.2459  0.1877
#> 4 0.0343 0.0640 0.5598 0.3838  0.3349

Each column is now a share of its channel’s ceiling, between 0 and 1.

Fit whatever model you like

mediamix stops here. The transformed columns are ordinary numeric vectors, so any modelling function will take them. Here lm() fits revenue on the five channels and the controls the data were simulated with (a weekly trend, price, the seasonal index and a December flag). The output sets the estimates against the true coefficients, then gives each estimate’s error in per cent:

model_data <- transformed
model_data$week <- seq_len(nrow(model_data))
model_data$price <- north$price
model_data$seasonality <- north$seasonality
model_data$holiday <- north$holiday

fit <- lm(north$revenue ~ ., data = model_data)
estimates <- rbind(estimate = coef(fit)[channels],
                   truth = truth$beta[channels])
round(estimates)
#>            tv video search social display
#> estimate 6013  1885   2622   2258     760
#> truth    5200  2400   4100   1800     900
round(100 * (estimates["estimate", ] / estimates["truth", ] - 1))
#>      tv   video  search  social display 
#>      16     -21     -36      25     -16

Close, not exact: the estimates miss the truth by between 16% and 36%. 156 weekly observations of flighted, mildly correlated media is a hard estimation problem, and pretending otherwise is how marketing mix models acquire their reputation.

The controls are doing real work. Drop them and the media coefficients absorb the trend and the price effect instead:

bare <- lm(north$revenue ~ ., data = transformed)
round(rbind(true = truth$beta[channels],
            with_controls = coef(fit)[channels],
            without = coef(bare)[channels]))
#>                 tv video search social display
#> true          5200  2400   4100   1800     900
#> with_controls 6013  1885   2622   2258     760
#> without       6110  1486   -218  -2067    2757

Without them 2 of the 5 media coefficients turn negative, and search collapses from 2622 to -218. Nothing about the transform changed; the specification did.

Contributions and ROI

A marketing mix deliverable is the decomposition rather than the coefficients: how much of predicted revenue each channel produced. contributions() multiplies each transformed channel by its coefficient, week by week, and pools everything else the model predicts into a "(baseline)" channel. Totals over the three years:

contrib <- contributions(transformed, fit, index = north$date)
round(tapply(contrib$contribution, contrib$channel, sum))
#> (baseline)    display     search     social         tv      video 
#>    3190425      40853     208307     132709     349629     102461

"(baseline)" is everything the model predicts that this decomposition does not attribute to the supplied media: the intercept, the trend, price, seasonality and the December uplift, pooled. It is not organic demand, and reporting it as such is a common way for one of these decks to overstate its own precision.

Pooling the rest into the baseline is what makes the arithmetic close exactly: in every week, the contributions sum to the model’s fitted value.

totals <- as.numeric(tapply(contrib$contribution, contrib$period, sum))
all.equal(totals, unname(fitted(fit)))
#> [1] TRUE

Media’s share of predicted revenue over the three years:

media_share <- 1 - sum(contrib$contribution[contrib$channel == "(baseline)"]) /
  sum(contrib$contribution)
round(media_share, 3)
#> [1] 0.207

Media accounts for 21% of predicted revenue here, and the baseline for the rest. Over time, with the baseline left out so the media is visible:

plot(contrib)

The dip at the very start of 2023 is the cold start: television’s long carryover takes weeks to fill from zero. adstock_steady_state() removes it when that matters, as vignette("carryover") shows.

roi() divides each channel’s total contribution by its total spend, which gives the average return per pound, and sorts the channels by it:

roi(contrib, north[channels])
#>   channel contribution  spend   roi
#> 1  social       132709  36716 3.614
#> 2  search       208307  74560 2.794
#> 3   video       102461  53248 1.924
#> 4 display        40853  26937 1.517
#> 5      tv       349629 266978 1.310

Average and marginal return are different questions

Average ROI is a scorecard. Marginal ROI, what the next pound returns, is the decision variable, and it is the only one of the two that should drive a reallocation.

The tempting shortcut is to differentiate the saturation curve at the mean adstocked level and multiply by the kernel’s first weight, 1 - decay, on the grounds that a pound spent this week only adds that much to this week’s adstock. It does, but it also adds to every later week’s adstock, and under a normalised kernel those contributions sum to the whole pound. The shortcut measures the return inside the week of spend and ignores the rest, which for a slow channel is most of it.

marginal_roi() avoids the calculus altogether. It re-runs the full transform on a budget 1% larger in every week and divides the extra response by the extra spend, the definition used by Jin et al. (2017) and by Google’s Meridian, so carryover and flighting are both handled by construction, and the result is a total over the same weeks as the average. Given the spend plan, the coefficients and spec, it does every channel at once:

marginal <- marginal_roi(north, coef(fit), spec = spec)
marginal[, c("channel", "roi", "mroi")]
#>   channel   roi   mroi
#> 1      tv 1.310 1.2534
#> 2   video 1.924 1.1961
#> 3  search 2.794 1.3490
#> 4  social 3.614 2.0892
#> 5 display 1.517 0.9324

Because both are totals over the observed weeks, response that the last weeks’ spend would produce after the data end is not counted. For a budget decision, the extend argument counts it; ?marginal_roi shows how much it matters.

Compare the shortcut for television, whose decay of 0.85 means only 15% of a week’s spend lands in that week’s adstock:

z_tv <- adstock_geometric(north$tv, decay = truth$decay[["tv"]])
shortcut <- mroi(mean(z_tv), coefficient = coef(fit)[["tv"]],
                 half_max = truth$half_max[["tv"]],
                 shape = truth$shape[["tv"]]) * (1 - truth$decay[["tv"]])
c(shortcut = shortcut, simulated = marginal$mroi[marginal$channel == "tv"])
#>  shortcut simulated 
#>    0.2059    1.2534

The shortcut understates television’s marginal return about 6-fold, and a reallocation built on it would strip budget from exactly the channel whose effect arrives late.

Read the mroi column of the marginal_roi() table instead. In this fitted model display’s average pound returns about 1.5, but its next pound returns 0.93, less than it costs, and the average-ROI table hides that completely. Search and social have average returns 2.1 and 1.7 times their marginal ones: concave curves, well up the slope. Television is the odd one out: its marginal return is close to its average, because its S-shaped curve (a shape of 1.6) is still near its steepest section at this budget. Under a concave curve marginal is below average everywhere; under an S-curve it can be close to or even above it below the inflection point, and assuming otherwise is how a threshold channel stays starved.

Every figure above comes from a model fitted to 156 noisy weeks. The data were simulated, so the fitted marginal returns can be set against the ones the true coefficients give:

true_marginal <- marginal_roi(north, truth$beta, spec = spec)
true_mroi <- stats::setNames(true_marginal$mroi, true_marginal$channel)
round(rbind(fitted = stats::setNames(marginal$mroi, marginal$channel),
            truth = true_mroi), 2)
#>          tv video search social display
#> fitted 1.25  1.20   1.35   2.09    0.93
#> truth  1.08  1.52   2.11   1.67    1.10

With the true coefficients display’s next pound returns 1.1, and the channels rank differently. Sampling noise in three years of weekly data is enough to move a marginal return across break-even, which is why a reallocation suggested by these numbers should be tested before it is made. The budget walkthrough on the package website puts bootstrap intervals on these marginal returns with block_bootstrap() and tests a reallocation before recommending one.

The response curve

response_curve() evaluates one channel’s fitted curve, its coefficient times its saturation curve, at a range of adstocked media levels, and gives the marginal return at each. Under a normalised kernel a steady weekly spend settles at the same adstocked level, so the spend axis can be read as sustained weekly spend. spend_for() inverts the curve: it returns the level that reaches a target response. For television:

curve <- response_curve(
  spend = seq(0, 6000, by = 1000),
  coefficient = coef(fit)[["tv"]],
  half_max = truth$half_max[["tv"]], shape = truth$shape[["tv"]]
)
curve
#>   spend response marginal
#> 1     0        0 0.001305
#> 2  1000     1290 1.621459
#> 3  2000     2724 1.191968
#> 4  3000     3686 0.760718
#> 5  4000     4300 0.489953
#> 6  5000     4702 0.327978
#> 7  6000     4977 0.228689

fine <- response_curve(seq(0, 6000, by = 50), coefficient = coef(fit)[["tv"]],
                       half_max = truth$half_max[["tv"]],
                       shape = truth$shape[["tv"]])
plot(fine, observed = adstock_geometric(north$tv, truth$decay[["tv"]]))


level <- spend_for(target = 3000, coefficient = coef(fit)[["tv"]],
                   half_max = truth$half_max[["tv"]],
                   shape = truth$shape[["tv"]])
level
#> [1] 2244

The marginal return peaks at a level of 900, where the S-shaped curve is steepest. The plot shades everything above 2302, the highest adstocked level in the data, as extrapolation. spend_for() puts a weekly response of 3000 at a level of 2244, near the top of the observed range.

These describe the curve the model fitted, which is not the same as what would happen if you actually spent that much. The curve is identified only over the range of spend the data contains; anything beyond it is extrapolation wearing a decimal point.
